title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
description: Grade 11 Biology: plant tissues (meristematic and permanent), complex tissues xylem and phloem, internal anatomy of root, stem and leaf, dicot vs monocot, and secondary growth.

topics.title: Plant Tissues: Meristematic and Permanent
topics.concept:
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of plants. The plant body is made of groups of similar cells called tissues. Based on whether they can divide, tissues are of two kinds: meristematic and permanent.

Meristematic tissues consist of actively dividing cells and are responsible for growth. By position they are: apical meristem (at the tips of root and shoot — increases length, i.e. primary growth), intercalary meristem (at the base of leaves/internodes, e.g. grasses) and lateral meristem (along the sides — vascular cambium and cork cambium, responsible for increase in girth, i.e. secondary growth).

Permanent tissues are made of cells that have lost the ability to divide and have taken on a fixed shape and function. They are of two types:

  • Simple permanent tissues (one cell type): parenchyma (thin-walled, living; for storage and photosynthesis), collenchyma (thickened at corners; gives flexible support to young stems) and sclerenchyma (thick, lignified, dead; gives mechanical strength — fibres and sclereids).
  • Complex permanent tissues (more than one cell type, work together for conduction): xylem and phloem, together called vascular tissue.

Xylem conducts water and minerals upward and gives support; its elements are tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma (vessels are absent in gymnosperms). Phloem conducts food (mostly downward); its elements are sieve tube cells, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma (companion cells are absent in gymnosperms).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three types of meristem by position and state the function of the lateral meristem.
examples.solution:
Meristems are classified by position.

  • Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems.
  • The lateral meristem (vascular and cork cambium) increases the girth of the plant (secondary growth).
examples.answer: Apical, intercalary and lateral; the lateral meristem increases girth (secondary growth).

examples.problem: Example 2: Differentiate parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma by their walls and function.
examples.solution:
These simple tissues differ in their cell walls.

  • Parenchyma: thin-walled, living; storage/photosynthesis.
  • Collenchyma: thickened at corners; flexible support.
  • Sclerenchyma: thick, lignified, dead; mechanical strength.
examples.answer: Parenchyma (thin walls, storage), collenchyma (corner-thickened, flexible support), sclerenchyma (lignified, dead, strength).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are xylem and phloem called complex tissues?
examples.solution:
Complex tissues have more than one cell type.

  • Xylem and phloem are each made of several kinds of cells working together.
  • They jointly perform conduction (water/food).
examples.answer: Because each is made of more than one type of cell working together to conduct materials.

recap:
• Anatomy = internal structure; tissues are meristematic (dividing) or permanent.
  • Meristems: apical (length), intercalary, lateral (girth).
  • Simple permanent: parenchyma (storage), collenchyma (flexible support), sclerenchyma (strength).
  • Complex permanent: xylem (water up) and phloem (food).

quiz.q: The meristem responsible for increase in the girth (thickness) of a plant is the:
quiz.explanation: The lateral meristem (cambium) increases girth — secondary growth.

quiz.q: Which tissue is dead, lignified and provides mechanical strength?
quiz.explanation: Sclerenchyma is thick-walled, lignified, dead and gives strength.

topics.title: Internal Anatomy of Root, Stem and Leaf
topics.concept:
The cells of a plant are organised into tissue systems: the epidermal (outer protective layer with cuticle, stomata, root hairs), the ground (cortex, pericycle, pith — storage and support) and the vascular (xylem and phloem) tissue systems. Their arrangement differs between organs and between dicots and monocots.

  • Dicot root — xylem and phloem in separate radial patches; usually 2–4 xylem groups (tetrarch); has a conjunctive tissue and a pericycle (which gives rise to lateral roots and the cambium).
  • Monocot root — similar but with many xylem groups (polyarch) and a large pith; no secondary growth.
  • Dicot stem — vascular bundles arranged in a ring, conjoint, open (with cambium between xylem and phloem, allowing secondary growth) and endarch.
  • Monocot stem — vascular bundles scattered in the ground tissue, conjoint, closed (no cambium, so no secondary growth), each surrounded by a sheath.
  • Leaf (dorsiventral, dicot) — upper and lower epidermis; mesophyll differentiated into palisade (column-like, photosynthetic) and spongy parenchyma; vascular bundles in the veins. Isobilateral (monocot) leaf — mesophyll not differentiated; stomata on both surfaces; some epidermal cells are large bulliform cells.

A simple rule to remember: in dicot stems the vascular bundles are in a ring and open (cambium present); in monocot stems they are scattered and closed (no cambium) — which is why monocots generally show no secondary growth.

examples.problem: Example 1: State two differences between a dicot stem and a monocot stem (anatomy).
examples.solution:
Compare vascular bundle arrangement and cambium.

  • Dicot stem: bundles in a ring, open (cambium present) → secondary growth.
  • Monocot stem: bundles scattered, closed (no cambium) → no secondary growth.
examples.answer: Dicot stem: bundles in a ring and open (with cambium, so secondary growth occurs); monocot stem: bundles scattered and closed (no cambium, no secondary growth).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between a dorsiventral and an isobilateral leaf?
examples.solution:
Leaves differ in mesophyll differentiation.

  • Dorsiventral (dicot): mesophyll has distinct palisade (upper) and spongy (lower) layers; stomata mainly on the lower surface.
  • Isobilateral (monocot): mesophyll is not differentiated; stomata on both surfaces.
examples.answer: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll with stomata mostly below; an isobilateral (monocot) leaf has undifferentiated mesophyll and stomata on both surfaces.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the three tissue systems of a plant.
examples.solution:
Tissues group into three systems.

  • Epidermal tissue system.
  • Ground tissue system.
  • Vascular tissue system.
examples.answer: The epidermal, the ground and the vascular tissue systems.

recap:
• Tissue systems: epidermal, ground, vascular.
  • Dicot stem: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open (cambium) → secondary growth.
  • Monocot stem: bundles scattered, closed (no cambium) → no secondary growth.
  • Dicot leaf = dorsiventral (palisade + spongy); monocot leaf = isobilateral (undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells).

quiz.q: In a monocot stem, the vascular bundles are:
quiz.explanation: Monocot stem bundles are scattered and closed (no cambium).

quiz.q: A leaf with palisade and spongy mesophyll and stomata mainly on the lower surface is:
quiz.explanation: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll.

topics.title: Secondary Growth
topics.concept:
Secondary growth is the increase in the girth (thickness) of a stem or root due to the activity of lateral meristems. It occurs mainly in dicots and gymnosperms (most monocots lack it). Two lateral meristems are involved:

  • Vascular cambium — forms a complete ring and divides to add new vascular tissue: secondary xylem towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside. Far more xylem is added than phloem, so most of a tree trunk is secondary xylem — this is what we call wood.
  • Cork cambium (phellogen) — develops in the cortex and produces cork (phellem) on the outside (a protective, waterproof, dead layer that forms the bark) and secondary cortex (phelloderm) on the inside. Small openings in the cork called lenticels allow gas exchange.

In trees of temperate or seasonal climates, the cambium is more active in spring (forming wide, light spring/early wood) and less active in winter/autumn (forming narrow, dark autumn/late wood). One ring of spring wood + one ring of autumn wood makes one annual ring. Counting the annual rings gives an estimate of the age of the tree — a science called dendrochronology.

The older, central wood becomes non-functional, darker and harder (heartwood, which gives mechanical support) while the outer, lighter wood remains functional in conduction (sapwood).

examples.problem: Example 1: What does the vascular cambium produce, and on which sides?
examples.solution:
The vascular cambium adds vascular tissue both ways.

  • It forms secondary xylem on the inner side.
  • It forms secondary phloem on the outer side (more xylem than phloem).
examples.answer: It produces secondary xylem (wood) towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside.

examples.problem: Example 2: How are annual rings formed, and how are they useful?
examples.solution:
Annual rings come from seasonal cambium activity.

  • Active spring growth (spring wood) + slower autumn growth (autumn wood) form one annual ring per year.
  • Counting the rings estimates the age of the tree.
examples.answer: Each year, spring wood and autumn wood form one annual ring; counting the rings estimates the tree's age.

examples.problem: Example 3: What are lenticels and what is their function?
examples.solution:
Lenticels are openings in the bark.

  • They are small pores formed in the cork.
  • They allow exchange of gases between the inside of the stem and the atmosphere.
examples.answer: Lenticels are small openings in the cork/bark that allow gas exchange between the stem and the air.

recap:
• Secondary growth = increase in girth by lateral meristems (dicots & gymnosperms).
  • Vascular cambium → secondary xylem (wood) inside, secondary phloem outside.
  • Cork cambium → cork/bark; lenticels allow gas exchange.
  • Annual rings (spring + autumn wood) estimate age; heartwood (support) vs sapwood (conduction).

quiz.q: Secondary growth (increase in girth) is mainly due to the:
quiz.explanation: Lateral meristems (vascular and cork cambium) cause secondary growth.

quiz.q: The bulk of a tree trunk (wood) is made of:
quiz.explanation: Most of the trunk is secondary xylem (wood), produced by the vascular cambium.

questions.q: The study of the internal structure of plants is:
questions.explanation: Anatomy studies internal structure.

questions.q: Tissues with actively dividing cells are:
questions.explanation: Meristematic tissues consist of dividing cells responsible for growth.

questions.q: The apical meristem is responsible for increase in:
questions.explanation: Apical meristems at the tips increase length (primary growth).

questions.q: Thin-walled living tissue mainly meant for storage is:
questions.explanation: Parenchyma is thin-walled, living and stores food.

questions.q: Dead, lignified cells giving mechanical strength form:
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma provides mechanical strength.

questions.q: Xylem and phloem are examples of ___ tissues.
questions.explanation: Xylem and phloem are complex (conducting) tissues.

questions.q: Xylem mainly conducts:
questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and minerals upward.

questions.q: In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles are:
options: Arranged in a ring, open (with cambium)
questions.explanation: Dicot stem bundles are in a ring and open (cambium present).

questions.q: Monocot stems usually show no secondary growth because their bundles are:
questions.explanation: Monocot bundles are closed (lack cambium), so no secondary growth.

questions.q: A dorsiventral leaf has mesophyll differentiated into palisade and:
questions.explanation: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll.

questions.q: Secondary growth increases the ___ of a plant.
questions.explanation: Secondary growth increases girth via lateral meristems.

questions.q: The vascular cambium forms secondary xylem on the ___ side.
questions.explanation: Secondary xylem (wood) is added to the inner side.

questions.q: Small openings in the bark that permit gas exchange are:
questions.explanation: Lenticels in the cork allow gas exchange.

questions.q: One annual ring is formed by:
options: One ring each of spring wood and autumn wood
questions.explanation: Spring wood + autumn wood make one annual ring per year.

questions.q: The darker, harder, non-conducting central wood that gives support is:
questions.explanation: Heartwood is the central, non-functional wood that gives support.

questions.q: Why can a dicot stem grow thicker over years while a typical monocot palm cannot?
options: Dicot stems have a vascular cambium (open bundles); monocots lack it (closed bundles)
questions.explanation: Open dicot bundles have cambium enabling secondary growth; closed monocot bundles do not.

questions.q: The trunk of an old tree is mostly secondary xylem because the cambium:
options: Adds far more xylem (inward) than phloem (outward)
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium produces much more secondary xylem than phloem, so wood dominates the trunk.

questions.q: Counting 30 annual rings in a tree trunk suggests the tree is about:
questions.explanation: Each annual ring represents one year's growth, so 30 rings ≈ 30 years.

questions.q: Collenchyma is well suited to support young, growing stems because it is:
options: Thickened yet living and flexible, so it bends without breaking
questions.explanation: Collenchyma's uneven living thickening gives flexible support that allows bending growth.

questions.q: A cross-section shows vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue with no cambium. The organ is a:
questions.explanation: Scattered, closed bundles with no cambium are the hallmark of a monocot stem.

questions.q: Bulliform cells in a monocot (e.g. grass) leaf help the plant by:
options: Rolling/folding the leaf to reduce water loss in dry conditions
questions.explanation: When water is scarce, bulliform cells lose turgor and the leaf rolls/folds, cutting transpiration.
